svg.data-steps: ["1976. Chester Wilk and four co plaintiffs file under Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act, two years after the Committee on Quackery was dissolved. Much of the litigation would turn on whether conduct that had formally ended was still producing effects.","1981. The first trial goes to the AMA and the case is all but over. Nothing that follows was inevitable: it continues only because the Seventh Circuit ordered a new trial.","1987. A bench trial before Judge Susan Getzendanner ends in a ruling that the AMA and certain members conspired unlawfully in restraint of trade. The remedy is a permanent injunction, no damages, and an order to print it in the journal of the association itself.","1990. The Seventh Circuit affirms on February 7 and the Supreme Court denies review later that year. Fourteen years from the filing to the last word.","And here is what fourteen years did not settle. The court expressly declined to rule on the validity or efficacy of chiropractic. Wilk won standing in the marketplace, not standing in science, and every brochure that begins with the words a federal court found is misreading it."]
svg.aria-label: Wilk against the AMA ran fourteen years, from filing in 1976 through a 1981 verdict for the AMA that nearly ended it, a new trial, the 1987 ruling and injunction, to affirmance in 1990, and it never decided whether chiropractic works.

g.text: the verdict stands and the case ends in 1981

g.data-tip: Five plaintiffs, led by a Chicago chiropractor, choosing a federal antitrust theory over defamation. That choice of statute was the single most important strategic decision in the case, because under it the plaintiffs never had to prove that chiropractic works.
g.text: Chester Wilk and four co plaintiffs

g.data-tip: A verdict for the AMA. Students who know only the 1987 headline miss that the case spent its first five years losing, and that everything afterwards depended on an appellate court agreeing to send it back.

g.text: the case continues to a second trial

g.data-tip: No jury this time. The ruling of September 25, 1987 is reported at 671 F. Supp. 1465. The patient care defense failed not because the court doubted the association's sincerity but because a boycott was more restrictive than necessary when publishing the evidence was available.

The shape of a remedy tells you what the court thought the wrong was. Damages would have said the plaintiffs were robbed of a quantified amount of business; an injunction says the conduct must stop and must be seen to have stopped.

Affirmed on February 7, 1990, with review denied later that year. The associational clause had already been revised out of the ethics code in 1980, so part of what this made permanent and enforceable was a change the association had already made.

The most tested point in this course. The court declined to rule on the validity or efficacy of chiropractic, so the judgment is evidence about a boycott and about nothing else. Standing in science was earned elsewhere and later, through the RAND consensus work and the 1994 acute low back pain guideline.
g.text: the court declined to rule on validity or efficacy
